title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) that isolates whether deterministic post‑processing (topology‑aware deterministic validator + lightweight simulator) changes a deterministic‑validator pass/fail verdict when both pipelines receive the identical single LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Design: 300 paired tasks, one shared LLM generation reused verbatim by both pipelines, primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Completed: 598 episodes → 299 analyzable pairs. Result (artifact‑grounded): n11 = 299, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). One preregistered pair was excluded after a provider failure; failure traces and all raw artifacts are archived and hashed. Conclusion: under shared_initial_candidate semantics and this synthetic task pool, deterministic post‑processing confirmed rather than changed the binary validator verdict for identical candidates. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and a full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest are archived for audit and replication.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, configuration repair, and operational playbooks. A common pipeline couples an LLM generator with deterministic post‑processing (validators, simulators, or formal checkers) to raise operational trustworthiness. However, when both pipelines receive the same LLM candidate, it is unclear whether improvements attributed to a tool‑augmented architecture come from changed generation (the generator) or from post‑processing (the verifier/simulator). We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory experiment to isolate the latter: when the identical candidate is supplied verbatim to both baseline and guarded pipelines (shared_initial_candidate semantics), does deterministic post‑processing change the binary deterministic‑validator verdict? We focus on operationally meaningful deterministic checks (reachability, make‑before‑break invariants, shutdown→change→restore patterns) implemented in an archived deterministic validator. The study strictly follows the preregistered plan cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 (SHA‑256: 991674d5...), and archives all artifacts and hashes for reproducibility.
sections.related_work: We situate this run relative to prior verified work on intent→configuration and tool‑augmented agents. Representative verified sources used to motivate the design include intent‑based configuration research (Nguyen et al., 2024; Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using LLMs, DOI:10.1002/nem.2313) and engineering reports on retrieval‑ or tool‑augmented agent paradigms (PreConfig, arXiv:2403.09369). Those works motivate verifier integration, verifier design constraints, and the need for reproducible, artifact‑hashed evaluations. Our contribution is methodological: a preregistered, artifact‑archived isolation of the post‑processing effect under shared candidate semantics — a question complementary to, not replacing, per‑condition independent generation experiments in prior literature.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 froze: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator pass indicator; shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM call per task reused verbatim by both pipelines); planned n=300 paired tasks (150 simple, 150 complex); analysis executor = paired_binary_analysis_v1; missingness/exclusion rules (complete‑pair handling; exact matches to public corpora moved to exploratory). Preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0 (archived). Experimental components (artifact pointers). - Generator: declared model gpt‑5‑mini; configuration and adapter are archived (execution/model_configuration.json — SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed... ). - Shared_initial generation: for each task a single LLM generation was produced and stored, then reused verbatim by both the baseline and guarded pipelines. Example: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256: 8f38c8be...). Provider trace for that call: execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (SHA‑256: fd046204...). - Deterministic validator/simulator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scorer id/version in each scoring JSON). The validator enforces workflow invariants (make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore, minimum‑active constraints), parses vendor‑agnostic CLI fragments, computes final_state snapshots, and emits binary pass/fail plus normalized_configuration and violation codes; all scoring outputs (execution/scoring/*.json) include validator_trace with final_state and difficulty metadata. Task corpus and sampling. Tasks were generated deterministically from a synthetic topology pool; each task manifest contains intent text, initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, and difficulty metadata (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; example excerpts referenced below). Stopping, failures, and retry policy. The preregistered maximum model‑call budget was 600 (one shared generation per task). The run stopped when all planned shared generations were attempted or the budget exhausted; one shared generation failed (pair‑000269) and was excluded per the preregistered complete‑pair rule — the provider failure is logged and the provider trace is archived (execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json; see execution manifest). Analysis plan. Primary analysis used the frozen paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor to compute the paired difference, two‑sided exact McNemar test, and paired bootstrap percentile CI (10k resamples, seed=1729). All analysis inputs/outputs are archived (analysis/*).
sections.results: Execution footprint and primary numeric outcome. Planned: 600 episodes (300 pairs). Completed: 598 episodes; failed: 2; analyzable complete pairs: 299 (execution/execution_manifest.json). Model calls used = 300 (one shared generation per task). The primary confirmatory artifact is analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256: d77df43abf...). Observed contingency: n11 = 299, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline success rate = 299/299 = 100.0%; guarded success rate = 299/299 = 100.0%. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed=1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Representative episode artifacts (all archived): - pair‑000001: shared candidate at execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8be...); scoring traces execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 6569b491...) and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 cefa6344...). - pair‑000002 and pair‑000003 are similarly archived (see execution/scoring/task-000002-*.json and execution/scoring/task-000003-*.json). Missingness and failures. One pair (pair‑000269) was excluded because the shared_initial generation provider call failed; the provider failure is recorded in execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json and in the execution log execution/execution_log.jsonl (both archived; see the execution manifest for file paths and SHA‑256s). No other exclusions were made. Secondary estimands. Because discordant pairs are zero, secondary exploratory estimands (simulated outage incidence, subgroup deltas) are uninformative in this shared‑candidate execution; raw latency and provider call counts remain archived for exploratory inspection (execution/provider_calls/* and execution/responses/*).
sections.discussion: Interpretation and limitations of inference. The archived, artifact‑grounded result — no discordant pairs among 299 complete pairs — shows that, for identical LLM candidates in this synthetic task distribution, deterministic post‑processing (validator + simulator) confirmed the binary validator verdict rather than changing it. This exact contingency (n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0) and the resulting degenerate bootstrap CI reflect a ceiling effect: the preregistered power calculation targeted a minimally important paired improvement of 0.20 assuming a baseline pass ≈ 0.60; the observed baseline = 1.00 makes that effect unobservable here. Practical implication: when generator candidates are already high‑quality under the evaluated distribution and validator specification, the operational role of the validator can be primarily auditative (providing normalized configurations, explicit violation codes, and final_state snapshots) rather than changing binary acceptance. However, this does not imply post‑processing is unnecessary — validators provide critical machine‑readable justifications and failure diagnostics archived in scoring traces (execution/scoring/*.json). Design guidance for follow‑ups (artifact‑grounded): (1) independent per‑condition generation (no shared candidates) to measure generation effects; (2) include adversarial or higher‑difficulty strata to avoid ceiling saturation; (3) replicate across multiple model families and seeds; (4) instrument repair‑loop ablations (iter=1 vs iter≥2) using the archived repair traces format. Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). - Internal validity: shared_initial semantics intentionally isolates post‑processing; it precludes attributing any effect to generator changes. - Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes explicit workflow invariants (documented in scoring JSONs); these invariants are operationally meaningful but not exhaustive of vendor/firmware behavior. - External validity: tasks are synthetic; generalization to production vendor CLIs, device idiosyncrasies, and operator policies requires replication with production artifacts. - Conclusion validity: ceiling effect limited hypothesis testing power for the preregistered minimally important effect. Reproducibility. All raw responses, provider traces, validator scoring JSONs (including validator_trace with final_state and violation lists), the full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest, the preregistration JSON (SHA‑256 991674d5...), and the master prompt archive (provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...) are archived. Representative artifact pointers (paths and SHA‑256s) are provided in the Disclosure and in the execution manifest to enable independent verification. Practical operational takeaways. - When planned deployments operate in a regime where generated candidates match operational invariants, validators still deliver critical audit trails and explicit violation encodings even if they do not alter binary accept decisions. - Evaluations that seek to quantify the end‑to‑end benefit of tool‑augmented agents must allow generation to differ across conditions and include adversarial strata to avoid the ceiling observed here.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a narrowly scoped experiment to test whether deterministic post‑processing changes a deterministic validator pass/fail verdict when identical LLM candidates are supplied to both pipelines. For 299 analyzable pairs the deterministic validator accepted the identical candidate in every pair (n11=299; no discordant pairs). The paired difference is 0.00 (McNemar p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). This artifact‑grounded result shows that in this synthetic, high‑quality generation regime post‑processing confirmed rather than changed the binary verdict; however, ceiling effects prevent broader conclusions about tool‑augmented generation benefits. We archive all raw artifacts, provider traces, scoring JSONs (validator_trace included), analysis inputs/outputs, and the master prompt SHA‑256 for audit and replication; recommended follow‑ups are independent per‑condition generation, adversarial task strata, and multi‑model replication.

limitations: This run used shared_initial_candidate semantics and therefore isolates only deterministic post‑processing for identical candidates; it cannot measure whether tool‑augmented generation (i.e., allowing the agent to call verifiers or simulators during generation or to produce repaired candidates) improves generation correctness.
Tasks were synthetic and executed in a lightweight topology simulator; external validity to vendor‑specific CLIs, firmware idiosyncrasies, or production telemetry is limited.
Only one declared model family (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families without replication.

The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) encodes curated workflow invariants and provides operationally meaningful checks, but it cannot exhaustively represent all production device behaviors or operator policies.
Observed baseline success = 100% produced a ceiling effect; the preregistered minimally important effect (0.20) was therefore unobservable in this run.
